accuracy.evidence: Number words one to ten spelt and ordered correctly everywhere (W array in flag_say.js, every item and explanation). Scope matches the topic and EYFS guidance: say the names to five, then to ten, plus counting back from five as in rocket and Five Little Ducks style rhymes. The adult text keeps reciting the string separate from one-to-one counting of objects, as in Gelman and Gallistel's stable-order principle, and describes Fuson's stable-but-unconventional portion (one, two, three, five) accurately.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented counting-string errors for 2 to 3 year olds: skipping a number (Bear's 'one, two, four' and 'one, two, three, four, six', challenge tag skip, p3, m8), saying a number twice ('one, two, three, three', tag twice, m3), going backwards when counting on (tag back), losing the order after five (step 4 to ten, m5) and thinking counting back goes up (tag up, rocket step prediction six vs four).

lab_distinct.evidence: flag_say.js is about the order of the spoken number string, not counting objects: a staircase that only accepts the next step and names a skip or repeat, a 1 to 5 train with a gap to fill, a 'spot Silly Bear's slip' strip of ducks with skip and repeat errors, a ten-stone frog track and a 5-to-1 rocket countdown. It passed the 30% shingle gate against every other flag lab, including flagdigit and flagpat.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each task practises one evidence statement of the topic: climbing five steps is saying 1 to 5 in order; the train makes the child choose the next name; fixing Bear's slips makes the child listen for skips and repeats; the frog track extends to ten; the rocket counts back. Tapping out of order is refused with a message naming the next number, so the child discovers the order and the done line confirms it.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option a toddler really gives: 'four' after one, two (skip); 'Yes, that is fine' for Bear's one, two, four; and 'six' after five when counting back (going up out of habit). Each is then tested on the canvas and the reveal states the right name.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions, every wrong choice tagged (skip, back, twice, fine, up, mix) with a specific message, e.g. 'That jumps over a number. Say every number, one at a time.' and 'Counting back goes down. Three, two, one!'. Choice order rotates each round so position is not a clue.

readability.evidence: Family audience: the kid text uses one- and two-syllable words in very short sentences and passes the FK 5.0 target; the adult text passes the 10.0 target and names each mistake in plain words. Every on-canvas label is a numeral with its word underneath, for pre-readers and the grown-up reading aloud.

no_filler.evidence: No filler phrases (gate passed). Every kid sentence is a count or a rule (no skips, no repeats, count back); adult paragraphs give scope, the normal learning path, named mistakes and the lab tour. Hints say exactly what to do, e.g. 'Say it slowly: one, two, three, …'.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots (390 px) in light and dark for every step before and after Show me: stairs, train carriages, three big choice tiles, duck cards and ten stones all fit without clipping; the action buttons below the canvas are full-size tap targets; numeral plus word stays readable at the smallest stone size.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (Say the next number, choice buttons for the gap, one button per duck, Say five for the rocket); the canvas aria-label is updated with every spoken message and the next number. Correctness is never shown by colour alone: text states 'Next is three' or names the slip. axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in light or dark on every step, before and after Show me, and the pipeline browser gate passed.
